Most gardeners throw their geraniums away at the end of the season — wasting perfectly healthy plants that could live for decades. The truth is, geraniums are incredibly resilient. Once you understand what really kills them in winter (hint: it’s not just the cold), you can keep them alive easily — no greenhouse, no fancy setup.

In this video, I’ll show you three proven methods to overwinter geraniums successfully so they come back bigger and bloom earlier every spring. You’ll see which method works best for your space, how to avoid the mistakes that kill most plants indoors, and how to wake them up next season stronger than ever.

– The Indoor Window Method — how to prune, transition, and care for plants in limited light without overwatering.
– The Cutting Propagation Method — how to turn one plant into twenty for free, and the secret to rooting success.
– The Hanging Dormancy Method — the old-fashioned trick that keeps geraniums alive for months without soil or water.

You’ll also learn the top three mistakes gardeners make — overwatering, bringing plants in too early, and panicking over leaf drop — and how to avoid them completely.

By the end of this video, you’ll know exactly how to prepare, store, and revive your geraniums so you never have to buy new ones again.

🌿 Subscribe for practical, real-world gardening advice that actually works — tested methods, step-by-step guides, and plant care strategies for every season.

- How to choose the right overwintering method for your home
- When to move geraniums before damaging frost
- How to inspect plants for pests before bringing them indoors
- How to keep potted geraniums growing under indoor light
- How to water indoor geraniums without keeping the roots constantly wet
- How bare-root geranium storage works

- How to read winter symptoms such as leaf loss, stretched growth, shriveling, or soft tissue
- How to restart stored plants in spring

Potted plants, bare-root plants, and cuttings need different winter care. A bright indoor geranium should not be treated like a bare-root plant in cool storage, and a leafless stored plant should not automatically be treated as dead.

That geranium you re-buy every single spring? The coleus, the fuchsia, those trailing things in your hanging baskets? You've been told they're annuals — one season and they're done. Toss 'em on the compost, buy new ones next year. 💸

Well… no. That's not true. Not even a little.

Those plants aren't annuals — they're perennials. They'd live for years and years, given the chance. The only reason they die on you is a hard frost. That's the whole story. And that means with about two minutes of work right now — before the cold hits — you can keep that exact plant alive through winter and turn it into three, four, five more, for absolutely nothing. 🌱

In this video I'll show you how to stop losing plants you never had to lose in the first place.

The best method of propagation of pelargonium.
Pinching geranium tips / removing the growing point / encouraging new shoots / growing a fuller, bushier plant.

Geranium propagation has become my favorite way to reset. Just me, a cutting, and a bit of soil. I love the simplicity of the ziplock method—it’s honest, no-fuss, and it works.

But I’ve learned that if you want a compact, bushy pelargonium, you can’t be afraid to pinch. It’s the constant back-and-forth—the pinching, the shaping, and the waiting—that builds the plant I actually want to live with. I’m moving away from just "growing" plants to actually designing how they fill my space.

It’s a small, quiet craft. I’m curious, do you also find yourself constantly adjusting the shape of your plants, or do you let them take their own course?

It’s amazing how a shared love for plants brings people together from all over the world, regardless of the language we speak. That’s why I translate my videos into multiple languages—if something isn’t clear, you can always turn on subtitles in your own language. And if this story resonated with you, please support me and my channel by hitting the like button and subscribing. That way, you won’t miss other episodes where I share my experience interacting with these amazing living beings we call plants.

That geranium you re-buy every single spring? The coleus, the fuchsia, those trailing things in your hanging baskets? You've been told they're annuals — one season and they're done. Toss 'em on the compost, buy new ones next year. 💸
